# The Right to be Forgotten Under GDPR

The "right to be forgotten" under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) permits individuals in the European Union to request the deletion or delisting of their personal data by organizations and search engines [1][3]. However, this right is not absolute and must be balanced against competing interests such as freedom of expression and public information access [1][3][10].

## Legal Origins and Primary Objectives

The right to be forgotten originated from a May 2014 ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union, which established that individuals can ask search engines like Google to delist specific query results related to their names [3]. It subsequently became a fundamental legal obligation codified under the GDPR to protect individual privacy rights and counter companies' refusal to delete out-of-date or harmful user data [2][7]. The objective is to safeguard data subjects by ensuring that personally identifiable information is removed when it no longer serves its original purpose [2][4].

## Conditions for Requesting Deletion Under Article 17

Under GDPR Article 17, also known as the right to erasure, individuals can request data deletion without undue delay under specific conditions [5]. Major grounds include data no longer being necessary for the original collection purpose, a data subject withdrawing consent when no other legal grounds for processing exist, an individual objecting to processing where there are no overriding legitimate grounds, or data having been unlawfully processed [4][5]. Data controllers are obligated to respond to these requests within 30 days [6].

## Exemptions and Exceptions to Erasure Requests

Article 17(3) outlines five explicit exceptions that allow organizations to legally refuse a right to be forgotten request even if a valid deletion ground is met [7]. These exemptions protect freedom of expression and information (covering journalism, academic, artistic, and literary expression), compliance with legal obligations or public-interest tasks (such as mandatory tax, employment, health, and financial retention periods), public health purposes like disease surveillance, and public safety or governmental purposes [7][8][9].

## Balancing Privacy Against Freedom of Expression and Public Interest

European courts balance the right to be forgotten against freedom of expression and the public's right to information by evaluating specific criteria [10][12]. These include the nature and seriousness of any criminal offenses, the status of legal proceedings, the data subject's involvement in public life, the public interest in the information, and the time elapsed since publication [10][12]. Under EU law, neither privacy nor freedom of expression automatically takes precedence, requiring a case-by-case judicial or operator assessment to reconcile fundamental rights [11].

## Compliance Challenges and Enforcement Trends for Multinational Tech Companies

Data protection enforcement has intensified, with regulators focusing on systematic enforcement, strict liability, and rigorous audits of data retention and minimization policies rather than just headline-grabbing fines [14][15]. Multinational companies operating in Europe face substantial compliance challenges regarding how they enforce internal data retention rules across systems, handle third-party relationships, and navigate evolving regulatory and enforcement trends [13][15].

## Conclusion

The right to be forgotten provides a vital mechanism for EU data subjects to reclaim control over their personal information [1][2]. Nonetheless, navigating its execution requires organizations to carefully balance privacy mandates against legal exceptions and fundamental rights to expression [7][11].

Article 17 is powerful but not unlimited. GDPR includes several exemptions, allowing organizations to refuse deletion under Article 17(3).

Data retained for journalistic, academic, or artistic expression may be exempt.

Organizations cannot delete data if required by law to keep it—for example, financial records for tax compliance.
